content: The process of updating the WHO recommendations on antenatal corticosteroid therapy involved several key steps: identifying priority questions and outcomes, gathering evidence, assessing and synthesizing the evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, evaluation of impact, and future updates. In 2021, the WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating these recommendations due to emerging evidence on the benefits and potential harms of antenatal corticosteroid therapy. Six main groups contributed to this process, each with specific roles: 1. Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG): This independent panel of 14 external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions (Africa, Americas, South-East Asia, Europe, Eastern Mediterranean, and Western Pacific) oversaw the process. 2. WHO Steering Group: Comprising WHO staff from the Departments of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research, and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, this group managed the update process. They drafted key recommendation questions in PICO format, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, and organized the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and External Review Group. They also supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis, finalized the recommendation document, and managed dissemination and impact assessment. 3. Guideline Development Group (GDG): This group included 18 external experts and stakeholders selected from a pool of approximately 50 experts in maternal and perinatal health. They reviewed evidence, formulated recommendations, and approved the final document during meetings held in January and February 2022. 4. Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG): This group, including guideline methodologists and systematic review teams, conducted or updated systematic reviews, appraised evidence, and developed evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. Experts from the Burnet Institute (Australia) and Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth (UK) contributed to this effort. 5. External Partners and Observers: Representatives from organizations such as USAID, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the International Pediatric Association (IPA) participated as observers. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO, were identified as key implementers of the recommendations. 6. External Review Group: Comprising five technical experts from four WHO regions, this group reviewed the recommendations for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance. Evidence to support the recommendations was derived from systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies. The WHO Steering Group collaborated with external systematic reviewers and methodologists to assess the relevance, timeliness, and quality of existing reviews. When necessary, new systematic reviews were commissioned. Evidence on effectiveness, values, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility was synthesized using the GRADE methodology and other tools, such as GRADE-CERQual for qualitative evidence. The GDG formulated recommendations using the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework, considering evidence on intervention effects, stakeholder values, resource use, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. Recommendations were classified into four categories: recommended, not recommended, recommended only in specific contexts, and recommended only in the context of rigorous research. This classification approach has been used for WHO maternal and perinatal health guidelines since 2016. The GDG meetings aimed to reach consensus on the recommendations, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the group, provided no strong objections were raised. The final recommendation document was prepared by the WHO Steering Group in collaboration with guideline methodologists, reflecting the deliberations and decisions of the GDG. It underwent external peer review by independent experts before publication.
